attacks.claim: Hold-ready texts show the library location, hold count, and a live single-use pickup code on the lock screen or message list. Combined with a readable card barcode, anyone holding the phone can collect the hold. The artifact has no minimal-preview option and no suppression of the body.
attacks.evidence: "Riverbend Library: 2 holds ready at Oak St locker. Code 482913, pick up by Sat Nov 14."

attacks.claim: A guardian's own phone can receive alerts about a minor's holds and pickup codes. The artifact does not say whether the teen or juvenile is told, whether they consent, or whether the guardian can see or stop this. This discloses a minor's library activity to a third party without a stated legal basis.
attacks.evidence: "guardians can opt in with their own number on the linked guardian account."

attacks.claim: Retention for the consent record, including IP address, is undefined while the flag is on. The 30-day deletion applies only on permanent withdrawal, so consent proof and IP data may be kept indefinitely.
attacks.evidence: "Phone number and consent record (timestamp, IP, checkbox text version) are stored in the patron record" and "Opt-in records are kept so turning the flag back on needs no re-consent."

attacks.claim: Locker access data (card identifier, cell, timestamp, wrong-PIN attempts) has no stated retention or access rule. Together with the notification log's patron id and branch, it can build a linkable record of when and where a patron collects holds, which the artifact does not reconcile with the no-borrowing-history policy.
attacks.evidence: ABSENT: retention and access rules for locker access and lockout logs; "purged after 30 days, consistent with our no-borrowing-history policy" covers only the notification log.

attacks.claim: Pickup codes sent by plaintext SMS are retained in provider message logs for 30 days. The artifact does not say whether codes are redacted from those logs.
attacks.evidence: "Code 482913, pick up by Sat Nov 14" with "it retains message logs 30 days"

attacks.claim: The opt-in flow sends a confirmation text to any submitted number with no stated rate limit, CAPTCHA, or per-number or per-account cap. Attackers with patron logins can drive SMS pumping or toll fraud, and the provider spend cap then halts texts for all cardholders.
attacks.evidence: "We send a confirmation text; texts start only after the patron replies YES." and "On cap, texts stop"

attacks.claim: The artifact does not describe re-verification or notice to the old number when a phone number changes after opt-in. An attacker with account access could redirect future hold codes and pickup notices to their own number.
attacks.evidence: ABSENT: re-verification, re-confirmation, or old-number notice when the phone number on the account changes.

attacks.claim: The link in the SMS has no scheme and the artifact does not say it is HTTPS-only. Patrons trust library texts, so a lookalike or downgraded link is an easy credential-phishing vector.
attacks.evidence: "Details: rpl.org/h."

attacks.claim: Webhook health is not monitored. Only signature failures alert, so an endpoint outage or stalled consumer would not page anyone while STOP requests are dropped. The artifact also gives no retry or reconciliation path for missed webhooks. The provider's own STOP handling mitigates some of the risk, but the gap in our flag state remains.
attacks.evidence: "Alerts: delivery failures > 5% for 15 min, webhook signature failures > 0" with "ABSENT: alert on zero webhooks received, processing lag, retry, or reconciliation."

attacks.claim: When the spend cap is reached, every opted-in patron falls back to email or phone calls at once. The only alert is at 70%, with no alert at cap-reached and no runbook, so ops learns of the switch only after the fact.
attacks.evidence: "Provider account hard spend cap $900/month, alert to ops at 70%. On cap, texts stop and every opted-in patron falls back"

attacks.claim: The fallback was tested only with a $5 cap in provider test mode. Email and automated phone-call fallback at production volume has no load or capacity validation.
attacks.evidence: "Spend cap reached (test cap $5) → fallback to email / phone call | Pass." ABSENT: production-scale load test of fallback channels.

attacks.claim: Lockers are promised 24/7, but a bank outage overnight has no defined patron fallback. The vendor on-site SLA is 4 hours and the service desk is closed outside opening hours.
attacks.evidence: "open 24/7 pickup lockers" with "vendor SLA 4 h on-site" and "Holds stay collectible at the service desk during opening hours"

attacks.claim: The locker_pickup rollback remaps holds but does not say what happens to codes already texted or loaded into cells. Single-use codes could still open cells after remap, or be dead while the patron is told a new location. The script was tested only on 1,200 rows.
attacks.evidence: "remapped to the branch desk by scripts/remap_locker_holds.sql (tested in staging on 1,200 rows)" with ABSENT: code invalidation and cell reconciliation.

attacks.claim: No retry, timeout, idempotency key, or duplicate-send protection is described for outbound texts that carry single-use pickup codes. Failed or repeated sends could lose codes or deliver duplicates, and the 08:00 queue flush has no throughput or backoff design.
attacks.evidence: "anything later is queued to 08:00." ABSENT: provider timeout, retry policy, idempotency key per notification, queue drain rate.

attacks.claim: QA covers only happy paths and the cap fallback. There is no fault injection for provider outage, carrier throttling, webhook downtime, locker controller offline, or ILS sync failure, which are the failures the monitoring section is meant to catch.
attacks.evidence: "against the production SMS provider account in test mode and a locker bank in the staff room." ABSENT: outage or fault-injection tests.

attacks.claim: The sms_holds rollback does not say what happens to texts already queued for 08:00 when the flag is switched off. They could still send after rollback or be silently dropped.
attacks.evidence: "sms_holds off: no new texts" with ABSENT: disposition of queued-but-unsent texts.

attacks.claim: The 09:00 flag flip for all 210k cardholders has no stated provider rate limits or expected launch-hour volume. A burst could breach provider limits before the 10:00 announcement and smoke test.
attacks.evidence: "Nov 9 09:00: flags on for all cardholders" with ABSENT: provider rate limits and launch-hour send volume.

attacks.claim: The opt-in can replace email, but the fallback sends SMS-only patrons to their "previous notice method" without saying what that is. If email was switched off, the fallback may send no alert, which contradicts "no alert is lost".
attacks.evidence: "in addition to (or instead of) the current email" and "no alert is lost"

attacks.claim: The public announcement overstates scope. Texts are opt-in and juvenile cards never see the option, but the announcement says "for every cardholder." It goes out publicly at 10:00 on launch day and cannot be recalled.
attacks.evidence: "Text alerts for holds, for every cardholder." versus "juvenile cards do not show it"

attacks.claim: The $900 hard cap and the cost model cover only SMS. The fallback sends automated phone calls to every opted-in patron, but those calls are neither costed nor capped, so the fallback could exceed the budget the cap is meant to protect.
attacks.evidence: "email or automated phone call" with the cost section covering only "38,000 texts/month at about $0.012"

attacks.claim: Spanish patrons get a Spanish version of the flow, but only the English disclosure is shown. The artifact does not show what Spanish-speaking patrons agree to.
attacks.evidence: "English and Spanish, following the patron's existing language preference." with only the English disclosure quoted.
